sources.title: Salif Keita (Q313318), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): label 'Salif Keita', description 'Malian singer-songwriter, referred to as the "Golden Voice of Africa"', born 25 August 1949, no death date, Korean label present, image 'Mali Salif Keita2 400.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Salif Keita', Britannica (revised 21 August 2025), read in full. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: a Malian singer-songwriter known for blending Mande traditions with jazz, rhythm and blues and other international styles to pioneer the Afropop dance-music genre; the move to Bamako, the Rail Band, Les Ambassadeurs du Motel in Abidjan, the move to Paris and the 1987 debut Soro, Amen (1991), the return to Bamako in 2001 and Moffou (2002), the 2005 foundation, La difference (2009), Tale (2012) and Un Autre blanc (2018) with the announced retirement from recording. Encyclopedia entry; it is editorial and uncited, and it also covers private-life context that is not scored.

Banning Eyre, 'Les Ambassadeurs du Motel de Bamako' (review of a two-CD compilation), Afropop Worldwide, 12 September 2014, read in full: Keita's 1971 arrival with the Rail Band, his wish to write songs that expressed Malian modernity in his own way, the 1973 move to the rival Les Ambassadeurs, the 1974 stadium showdown between the two bands, the band's variety repertoire, the 1977 trip to Abidjan, and the track-by-track account of his vocals and composing credits. Specialist music journalism by an author who has also interviewed Keita; it draws on sleeve notes and on Keita's own interviews.

Nigel Williamson, 'Les Ambassadeurs du Motel de Bamako' (five-star review), Songlines, November/December 2014, read in full (one paragraph): the band and the Rail Band as the foundation of popular Malian music, the 1975-1977 recordings, Keita singing exactly half of the 18 tracks, and the contribution of the singer Ousmane Dia and of the guitarists, organist and horn section. Independent review that places Keita as part of an ensemble.

Lucas Keen, 'The story of Salif Keita's Soro' (a conversation with the producer Francois Breant), Pan African Music magazine, 14 December 2021, read in full: the 1987 album recorded at Studio Harry Son in Paris, the pan-African team of players, Breant's account of Keita singing demos and mic tests 'like it was the last time of his life', the use of synthesisers to imitate traditional instruments, the cultural advice Keita and the executive producer gave, and the claim that the record baffled listeners who expected African music to be 'a museum'. An anniversary feature built mainly on the producer's recollection, so it is an insider and retrospective account.

Robert Christgau, Consumer Guide review of Salif Keita, 'Soro' (Mango, 1987), read in full (about 250 words, grade B): calls him one of Africa's great singers but judges him short of Youssou N'Dour's purity and range, says he compensates with experience, feeling and authority, and says the Paris arrangements 'sacrifice a quantum of groove for dramatic effects'. Contemporary critical counter-voice from a US rock critic; short and opinionated.

Banning Eyre, 'Salif Keita Gives His Blessing And Takes A Final Bow With Un Autre Blanc', NPR All Things Considered, 20 March 2019, read in full (the page text of the review): about 25 albums over a 40-year career, Soro as the album that introduced his voice, the retirement from recording, and the guests on the final album (Angelique Kidjo, Ladysmith Black Mambazo). Short broadcast review; the audio was not listened to.

Banning Eyre, 'Salif Keita Speaks Out on His Career, Mali's Crisis and Retirement', Afropop Worldwide, 22 December 2014, read in full (about 3,000 words of interview): the Tale album and its arranger, the ten reunion shows with Les Ambassadeurs, his naming of the Rail Band guitarists Djelimady Tounkara and Kante Manfila as his teachers, his loyalty to his long-time guitarist, his stated plan to retire, and his views on young Malian music. Interview, so mainly first-person; the passages on national politics are context and are not scored.

Banning Eyre, 'Salif Keita talks going acoustic with So Kono', Afropop Worldwide, 23 April 2025, read about two thirds (introduction and the song-by-song portion): his earlier retirement statements and the return to a solo acoustic album recorded in a hotel room in Japan in 2023, the producer's persuasion, and the dedications to a patron, a friend and his former guitarist. Interview, mostly first-person; the political discussion is context and is not scored.

Frank Bessem, 'Salif Keita (& les Ambassadeurs)', Musiques d'Afrique (musiques-afrique.net), read in full: a career outline from the Rail Band (1970) and Les Ambassadeurs (1973) through the Abidjan years, the 1984 move to France, Soro, the return to Bamako and the semi-acoustic Moffou, a note that he created the Moffou club, cultural centre and recording studio to promote young artists, a discography, and the opinion that the later Paris albums 'lack more and more the African feel'. Enthusiast web guide by a single author; it is used for the outline, the Moffou venture and one critical judgement.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_sk_eb, src_sk_afropop_amb, src_sk_pam, src_sk_christgau | 1973-1987 | encyclopedia + specialist review + producer feature + critic] Britannica says he blended Mande traditions, especially hunters' songs, with jazz, rhythm and blues and rock to pioneer Afropop dance music, and Afropop says he left the Rail Band wanting to write songs that expressed Malian modernity in his own way; the producer's account stresses layered synthesised imitations of traditional instruments on Soro. Christgau, a contemporary critic, grants authority but finds the arrangements trade groove for effect, so the originality is of synthesis rather than of a wholly new form. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 74 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.58 because the 'pioneer' wording is Britannica's editorial characterisation and the detailed account of Soro comes from the producer's own retrospective, while the one contemporary critic is lukewarm.

experimentation.rationale: [src_sk_eb, src_sk_afropop14, src_sk_afropop25, src_sk_musafr | 1987-2025 | encyclopedia + two interviews + enthusiast guide] Britannica describes the stylistic range of successive albums (Moffou with guests from many acoustic traditions, Tale with trance, dub and hip-hop elements, the personal Un Autre blanc), and in 2014 he said he wanted this time to go outside his recent calm style and make people dance, with an electric arranger; in 2025 he made a solo acoustic record after saying he would not. The interviews are first-person and the albums' reception is mixed, so the pattern is reasoned from the discography rather than from independent analysis of each change.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_sk_pam, src_sk_afropop_amb, src_sk_afropop14, src_sk_songlines | 1971-2014 | producer feature + specialist review + interview + review] The producer says Keita sang demos and mic tests 'like it was the last time of his life', which is a specific working-habit observation; Afropop notes he treated the move to Les Ambassadeurs as schooling among more 'intellectual' musicians, and in 2014 he named the Rail Band and Ambassadeurs guitarists as the people who taught him his craft. The producer is an insider recalling thirty-four years later, and the other items are partly Keita's own account.

adaptability.rationale: [src_sk_eb, src_sk_musafr, src_sk_afropop_amb | 1971-2025 | encyclopedia + enthusiast guide + specialist review] He moved from Bamako nightclubs to the Rail Band, to Les Ambassadeurs, to Abidjan, to a solo career in Paris, back to Bamako in 2001, and later to acoustic ensembles and a solo acoustic album; the sources describe these moves in sequence and the music changing with each setting. The reasons for each move are given only partly and some of them involve factors outside music, so the row rests on the documented sequence rather than on stated motives.

collaboration.rationale: [src_sk_eb, src_sk_pam, src_sk_npr19, src_sk_afropop14, src_sk_songlines | 1973-2018 | encyclopedia + producer feature + broadcast review + interview + review] Les Ambassadeurs was a multinational variety band in which he sang half of the 18 compiled tracks beside other singers, Moffou and Tale featured guests such as Bobby McFerrin and Esperanza Spalding, Un Autre blanc features Angelique Kidjo and Ladysmith Black Mambazo, and in 2014 he reunited the old band members for ten shows and spoke of a long loyalty to his guitarist. The Soro producer reports that Keita arrived with a group of friends to judge him. The guest and reunion evidence is documented; how he collaborated day to day is seen mostly through his own and the producer's accounts.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_sk_afropop_amb, src_sk_eb, src_sk_pam | 1973-1987 | specialist review + encyclopedia + producer feature] Afropop reports that he left the established Rail Band for a new rival band in 1973, that the band left Mali for Abidjan, and the producer says Soro 'baffled' listeners who expected traditional African music. These are career bets whose outcome was successful, but the sources do not show him weighing the risk, and the Abidjan move involved wider circumstances, so confidence is moderate.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_sk_afropop_amb, src_sk_eb, src_sk_musafr | 1973-1984 | specialist review + encyclopedia + enthusiast guide] Afropop says the Rail Band job began to feel like a trap because he wanted to write songs of his own, which is the stated reason for the 1973 move, and Britannica and the guide report the move to Paris to build a solo career. The row relies on one interpretive reading in the Afropop review plus the career sequence; the family and social background in Britannica is not used.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_sk_musafr, src_sk_afropop25 | 2002-2025 | enthusiast guide + interview] The guide reports that after returning to Bamako he built the Moffou club, cultural centre and studio to promote young artists, and the 2025 interview describes songs written to honour a patron's donations; the cultural-centre claim rests on a single web guide and the interview items are his own descriptions of songs, so this is a modest inference. The foundation and any advocacy are deliberately not scored.
